idiom_name: ActiveSupport::Notifications (instrument/subscribe on a process-wide Fanout registry)
implementation_notes: ActiveSupport::Notifications supplies the hub as a process-wide Fanout registry keyed by event name: instrument('order.placed', payload) executes the block and then notifies every subscriber, subscribe('order.placed') (or a Regexp, or no argument for all events) registers a block or a callable object, subscribe returns a subscriber handle and unsubscribe(handle) or unsubscribe(name) removes it, and subscribed(callback, name) { } gives a temporary registration that is released automatically. Subscribers receive an event object with name/duration/payload/allocations or the five positional arguments; the payload carries the context, and failures are surfaced through the payload's :exception keys. A hand-written hub - a Hash mapping names to arrays of callables, plus a dispatch loop - remains the right choice outside Rails (or with the dry-events gem) when the process-wide registry, its caches and its name-based unsubscribe semantics are unwanted.
code_sketch:
# publish: subscribers run after the block returns
ActiveSupport::Notifications.instrument('order.placed', order_id: 42) do
  Orders.create!(id: 42)
end

subscriber = ActiveSupport::Notifications.subscribe('order.placed') do |event|
  Billing.handle(event.payload[:order_id], duration: event.duration)
end

ActiveSupport::Notifications.unsubscribe(subscriber)
pitfalls: instrument notifies synchronously in the instrumenter's stack, so a slow subscriber slows every caller of instrument - the framework warns to keep subscribers lean.
unsubscribe('order.placed') removes all subscriptions with that name, while unsubscribing a subscriber object is the API to use for a single handler, and it also purges internal caches.
Regexp subscribers stay subscribed to everything they match unless a matching event name is passed to unsubscribe, which makes partial teardown easy to get wrong.
The registry is process-global: subscribers registered in an initializer or a spec leak across tests and accumulate in long-running processes.
